pos: n. (one who labours together with another in the gospel; Paul's ordinary title for those who worked beside him)
etymology: English fellow, a companion or partner, with labourer. The Greek sunergos is a compound — one who works together — and Paul uses it of men, of women, and once of himself and God.
biblical_def: Paul rarely calls anyone an assistant. He calls them fellowlabourers. Of Timothy: “And sent Timotheus, our brother, and minister of God, and our fellowlabourer in the gospel of Christ, to establish you, and to comfort you concerning your faith” (1Th 3:2). Of the man who owned the runaway slave: “Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, and Timothy our brother, unto Philemon our dearly beloved, and fellowlabourer” (Phm 1:1). At the close of the same short letter he names four more: “Marcus, Aristarchus, Demas, Lucas, my fellowlabourers” (Phm 1:24) — and one of those four would afterward forsake him, having loved this present world, which the apostle records without erasing the earlier commendation. Colossians calls a small group of Jewish believers “my fellowworkers unto the kingdom of God, which have been a comfort unto me” (Col 4:11). And the highest use of the word makes the whole church a work-site under one Owner: “For we are labourers together with God: ye are God's husbandry, ye are God's building” (1Co 3:9). The gospel is described throughout as labour — not a platform, not an office, but work done alongside other men.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives fellow-laborer as one who labors in the same business or design; and labourer as one who works, particularly one whose work requires bodily strength or constant application.
webster_full: FELLOW, n. A companion; an associate.
2. One of the same kind; an equal in rank or condition.
FELLOW-LABORER, n. One who labors in the same business or design.
Our fellowlabourer in the gospel of Christ. 1 Thess. iii.
scriptures: And sent Timotheus, our brother, and minister of God, and our fellowlabourer in the gospel of Christ, to establish you, and to comfort you concerning your faith:
Phm 1:1
Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, and Timothy our brother, unto Philemon our dearly beloved, and fellowlabourer,
Phm 1:24
Marcus, Aristarchus, Demas, Lucas, my fellowlabourers.
For we are labourers together with God: ye are God's husbandry, ye are God's building.
corruption_summary: Ministry has been reorganised around personalities and platforms, while the apostle's standing vocabulary for the work is a crew of men labouring together.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul's letters end in lists of names, and the lists are doctrine. He is the apostle to the Gentiles, he has seen the Lord, and he writes Scripture; and he calls a householder in Colosse his fellowlabourer and a young man from Lystra his brother and fellowlabourer in the gospel. There is a real and unrepeatable apostolic office in the New Testament, and the same New Testament shows that office surrounded by ordinary workers who are named, thanked and trusted with errands that mattered. Set beside that the arrangement now common, in which a ministry is built around one gifted man, his name on the building, his face on the material, and everyone else classed as staff or volunteers. The structure is not merely unwise; it contradicts the apostle's own account of how the work is done and who is doing it.

The list at Philemon 24 is worth reading slowly for a second reason. Demas is in it. In a later letter Paul writes that Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world, and is departed unto Thessalonica — and the earlier commendation stands in the canon unaltered. Two things follow. The first is that a man may be a genuine fellowlabourer for years and afterwards go; profession is not perseverance, and the church is right to be sober about it. The second is that Paul does not retroactively deny the earlier labour or rewrite the record to protect himself from having endorsed a man who fell. That honesty is rare. Where a leader departs today, ministries commonly erase him from the history entirely, which is neither charitable nor truthful. Scripture's way is to name what was, name what happened, and leave both standing.
roots_summary: Greek sunergos (G4904), a fellow worker, from sun, together, and ergon, work; rendered fellowlabourer, fellowworker, and helper throughout the epistles.
roots_lines: Greek sunergos (G4904) — a fellow worker; used of Timothy, Philemon, Titus, Priscilla and Aquila, and of the church with God; 1 Thessalonians 3:2, Romans 16:3.
Greek ergon (G2041) — work, deed, labour; the root that makes ministry a trade rather than a title.
Greek kopos (G2873) — toil to the point of weariness; the labour of love which God is not unrighteous to forget; Hebrews 6:10.
Greek georgion (G1091) — a tilled field, husbandry; ye are God's husbandry; 1 Corinthians 3:9.
Greek diakonos (G1249) — a servant, minister; Timothy is minister of God and fellowlabourer in one clause; 1 Thessalonians 3:2.
usage: “Our fellowlabourer in the gospel of Christ” — the apostle's ordinary word for a colleague.
“Marcus, Aristarchus, Demas, Lucas, my fellowlabourers” — and one of the four would go.
“We are labourers together with God” — the work-site and its Owner.

pos: n. (one imprisoned along with another for the gospel's sake)
etymology: English fellow with prisoner. The Greek sunaichmalotos is stronger than the English: literally a fellow captive taken at the spear's point, a prisoner of war.
biblical_def: Twice Paul gives this title, both times from confinement. “Aristarchus my fellowprisoner saluteth you, and Marcus, sister's son to Barnabas” (Col 4:10); and “There salute thee Epaphras, my fellowprisoner in Christ Jesus” (Phm 1:23). Aristarchus was the Thessalonian who had been seized in the theatre at Ephesus and who later sailed with Paul toward Rome (Act 20:4); Epaphras was the man who had first preached to the Colossians and who laboured fervently in prayer for them. The Greek word is martial — a captive taken in war — and Paul's use of it is deliberate, for he never speaks of his chains as an accident of Roman administration. He is a prisoner of Jesus Christ (Phm 1:1), which locates his captivity under a different jurisdiction than Caesar's. The men beside him share the same status. Rome supposed it was holding a troublesome Jew and two companions; the letters written out of that cell have outlived the empire that issued the sentence.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a prisoner as one who is confined in a prison by lawful authority, and one who is deprived of liberty in any manner; a fellow-prisoner shares the same confinement.
webster_full: PRISONER, n. One who is confined in a prison by legal arrest or warrant.
2. A person under arrest or in custody, whether in prison or not.
3. A captive; one taken by an enemy in war.
Epaphras, my fellowprisoner in Christ Jesus. Philem. 23.
scriptures: Col 4:10
Aristarchus my fellowprisoner saluteth you, and Marcus, sister's son to Barnabas, (touching whom ye received commandments: if he come unto you, receive him;)
Phm 1:23
There salute thee Epaphras, my fellowprisoner in Christ Jesus;
Phm 1:1
Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, and Timothy our brother, unto Philemon our dearly beloved, and fellowlabourer,
Act 20:4
And there accompanied him into Asia Sopater of Berea; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timotheus; and of Asia, Tychicus and Trophimus.
corruption_summary: Imprisonment for the faith is treated as a first-century antique or a distant emergency, though the New Testament assumes it as a normal cost and names the men who paid it.
corruption_paragraphs: The New Testament does not present prison as a catastrophe that derailed the mission. Four of Paul's letters were written from confinement, and in them he says the things which happened unto him have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel, because his bonds in Christ were manifest in all the palace. That is not stoicism; it is a doctrine of providence applied to a cell. The modern habit is to treat the imprisonment of Christians as an exception requiring urgent explanation — something has gone wrong, someone has failed — whereas the apostles treat it as within the ordinary run of a faithful ministry. Hebrews commands the church to remember them that are in bonds as bound with them, which is exactly the sense of Paul's word: not sympathy from outside, but a shared status.

The second thing the word does is name the men. Aristarchus is not a symbol; he is a Thessalonian who was dragged into a theatre by a mob at Ephesus, who accompanied Paul into Asia, who sailed with him toward Rome, and who is greeting a congregation from a prison at the end of a letter. Epaphras had carried the gospel to Colosse and is described in the same letter as always labouring fervently for them in prayers. Church history is full of such names and the church is poor at keeping them. Where a congregation knows the names of its own imprisoned brethren in other lands and prays for them by name, Hebrews 13:3 is being obeyed; where the suffering church is a category rather than a list of persons, it is not.
roots_summary: Greek sunaichmalotos (G4869), a fellow captive of war, from sun, together, and aichmalotos, one taken at the spear point; with desmios (G1198), a prisoner in bonds.
roots_lines: Greek sunaichmalotos (G4869) — a fellow prisoner of war; used of Aristarchus, Epaphras, and Andronicus and Junia; Colossians 4:10, Romans 16:7.
Greek aichmalotos (G164) — a captive taken by the spear; he led captivity captive; Ephesians 4:8.
Greek desmios (G1198) — one in bonds; Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ; Philemon 1:1.
Greek desmos (G1199) — a band, a chain; my bonds in Christ are manifest in all the palace; Philippians 1:13.
Greek sumpatheo (G4834) — to suffer with; remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them; Hebrews 13:3.
usage: “Aristarchus my fellowprisoner saluteth you” — greetings written from a cell.
“Epaphras, my fellowprisoner in Christ Jesus” — the jurisdiction named.
“Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ” — not of Caesar, though Caesar held the key.

pos: n. (one who serves in the same warfare; Paul's title for two men, one a messenger and one a household elder)
etymology: English fellow with soldier, from Old French soldier, one who serves for pay. The Greek sustratiotes is a fellow campaigner — a man in the same ranks, under the same commander.
biblical_def: Paul gives the title twice, and both men are unexpected choices. Epaphroditus: “Yet I supposed it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my brother, and companion in labour, and fellowsoldier, but your messenger, and he that ministered to my wants” (Php 2:25). He had carried a gift from Philippi to Rome and nearly died doing it — the next verses say he was sick nigh unto death, and that he longed after them and was full of heaviness because they had heard of it (Php 2:26). His soldiering was a journey with a purse and a sickbed at the end of it. Archippus: “And to our beloved Apphia, and Archippus our fellowsoldier, and to the church in thy house” (Phm 1:2) — named in a household letter about a runaway slave, and charged in Colossians to take heed to the ministry he had received. The military figure runs through Paul: “Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ” (2Ti 2:3), and the armour is God's, not the man's (Eph 6:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a soldier as a man engaged in military service, and particularly a brave warrior; a fellow-soldier is one who serves in the same army or campaign.
webster_full: SOLDIER, n. A man engaged in military service; one whose occupation is military; a man enlisted for service in an army.
2. Emphatically, a brave warrior; a man of military experience and skill.
FELLOW-SOLDIER, n. One who serves in the same army.
Archippus our fellowsoldier. Philem. 2.
scriptures: Php 2:25
Yet I supposed it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my brother, and companion in labour, and fellowsoldier, but your messenger, and he that ministered to my wants.
Phm 1:2
And to our beloved Apphia, and Archippus our fellowsoldier, and to the church in thy house:
Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ.
Eph 6:11
Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.
corruption_summary: Military language in the Christian life is either dropped as unkind or picked up as a licence for combativeness toward men, when Paul gives the title to a sick messenger and a house-church elder.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite mishandlings of this figure are common. The first is embarrassment: soldiering language is thought harsh and is quietly retired from hymnals and preaching. That cannot be squared with an apostle who writes of armour, weapons, warfare, a good fight and a crown, or with a Lord who told men to count the cost as a king going to war. The Christian life is described as a conflict because it is one. The second mishandling is worse, because it keeps the language and misdirects it: the warfare is turned on other people — rival congregations, cultural opponents, brethren who differ — and pugnacity is baptised as courage. Paul settles the aim explicitly: we wrestle not against flesh and blood, and the weapons of our warfare are not carnal. The armour of Ephesians 6 is nearly all defensive, and the one offensive weapon is the word of God.

It is worth marking whom Paul actually calls a fellowsoldier. Epaphroditus carried money and letters, fell dangerously ill, and was more distressed that Philippi had heard of his sickness than about the sickness itself; Paul tells the church to receive him with gladness and to hold such in reputation, because for the work of Christ he was nigh unto death, not regarding his life. That is the soldiering commended: an errand carried through at cost, on behalf of others, without heroics. Archippus is named in the greeting of a private letter and told elsewhere to fulfil his ministry — a man of one household and one congregation. The New Testament does not reserve the title for those in visible combat. It gives it to men who stayed at their post.
roots_summary: Greek sustratiotes (G4961), a fellow soldier, from sun and stratiotes; with strateuomai (G4754), to serve as a soldier, and panoplia (G3833), the whole armour.
roots_lines: Greek sustratiotes (G4961) — a fellow soldier; used only of Epaphroditus and Archippus; Philippians 2:25, Philemon 1:2.
Greek stratiotes (G4757) — a soldier; endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ; 2 Timothy 2:3.
Greek strateia (G4752) — warfare, a campaign; the weapons of our warfare are not carnal; 2 Corinthians 10:4.
Greek panoplia (G3833) — full armour; put on the whole armour of God; Ephesians 6:11.
Greek apostolos (G652) — one sent; rendered messenger of Epaphroditus in the same verse as fellowsoldier; Philippians 2:25.
usage: “My brother, and companion in labour, and fellowsoldier” — of a man who carried a purse and nearly died.
“Archippus our fellowsoldier” — named in a letter about a runaway slave.
“Endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ” — the whole of the commission.

pos: n. (a partner in the same work; the Authorized Version's plainest rendering of Paul's sunergos)
etymology: English work with fellow, a partner. The Greek is the same sunergos elsewhere translated fellowlabourer and fellowworker; the translators varied the English rather than the sense.
biblical_def: The word occurs once: “Timotheus my workfellow, and Lucius, and Jason, and Sosipater, my kinsmen, salute you” (Rom 16:21). It stands in the greatest list of names in the New Testament, Romans 16, where Paul salutes some thirty persons in a church he had never visited and mentions their labours by name — Phebe a servant of the church at Cenchrea, Priscilla and Aquila who laid down their own necks, Mary who bestowed much labour, Andronicus and Junia his kinsmen and fellowprisoners, Tryphena and Tryphosa who laboured in the Lord. The chapter is often skipped in reading and it is one of the most instructive in the epistle, because it shows what the doctrine of the preceding fifteen chapters produced: a network of ordinary believers, Jew and Gentile, bond and free, men and women, whose names the apostle knew. Colossians uses the same Greek word of a small remnant: “These only are my fellowworkers unto the kingdom of God, which have been a comfort unto me” (Col 4:11), and 1 Corinthians lifts it highest: “we are labourers together with God” (1Co 3:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives work-fellow as one engaged in the same work with another; a companion in labor.
webster_full: WORK, n. Labor; employment; exertion of strength; particularly in man, manual labor.
WORK-FELLOW, n. One engaged in the same work with another.
Timotheus my workfellow. Rom. xvi.
WORKMAN, n. Any man employed in labor, whether in agriculture or manufactures.
scriptures: Timotheus my workfellow, and Lucius, and Jason, and Sosipater, my kinsmen, salute you.
Col 4:11
And Jesus, which is called Justus, who are of the circumcision. These only are my fellowworkers unto the kingdom of God, which have been a comfort unto me.
For we are labourers together with God: ye are God's husbandry, ye are God's building.
Act 20:4
And there accompanied him into Asia Sopater of Berea; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timotheus; and of Asia, Tychicus and Trophimus.
corruption_summary: Romans 16 is treated as an appendix of names with no doctrine in it, when it is the visible result of the doctrine and the apostle's own model of a church.
corruption_paragraphs: It is a curiosity of modern preaching that Romans is expounded chapter by chapter with great care through justification, union with Christ, election and the ingrafting of Israel, and then stops. Chapter 16 is passed over as a list. But the list is the point of arrival. A gospel that produces no named people in no particular city has not been believed by anyone; the chapter shows the doctrine of chapters one to eleven and the exhortations of twelve to fifteen taking flesh in Phebe, Epaenetus, Urbane, Apelles, the household of Narcissus and the rest. Paul had not yet been to Rome, and he knew their names, their work and their households. That is a rebuke to two things at once: to a doctrinal Christianity with no people in it, and to a busy congregational life in which nobody could produce thirty names with a sentence of true commendation attached to each.

The word itself is worth defending against a common flattening. Workfellow, fellowlabourer and fellowworker render one Greek word, and the Authorized Version's variety is sometimes charged as inconsistency. It is better understood as the ordinary liberty of a translation that renders sense rather than mechanically matching one English word to one Greek word — a liberty every faithful translation must take somewhere, since languages do not map one to one. The doctrine of verbal inspiration concerns the original text God gave, and it is honoured, not compromised, by careful translation. What must never happen is what happened in the July batches of this very dictionary: a quotation labelled as one version silently carrying the wording of another. Variety in rendering is a translator's judgment, openly made; misattribution is a false witness.
roots_summary: Greek sunergos (G4904), a fellow worker — rendered workfellow at Romans 16:21, fellowlabourer in Thessalonians and Philemon, and fellowworker in Colossians.
roots_lines: Greek sunergos (G4904) — one who works together; the single word behind three English renderings; Romans 16:21, Colossians 4:11.
Greek sungenes (G4773) — kinsman, of the same race; Lucius, Jason and Sosipater are so named in the same verse; Romans 16:21.
Greek kopiao (G2872) — to labour to weariness; used of Mary, Tryphena, Tryphosa and Persis in the same chapter; Romans 16:6, Romans 16:12.
Greek diakonos (G1249) — a servant; Phebe a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea; Romans 16:1.
Greek oikodome (G3619) — a building, edification; ye are God's building; 1 Corinthians 3:9.
usage: “Timotheus my workfellow” — one Greek word, three English renderings.
“These only are my fellowworkers unto the kingdom of God” — a short list, and a comfort.
Romans 16 — the doctrine of the first fifteen chapters, with names attached.

pos: n. pl. (men of one's own nation; in the New Testament, chiefly those from whom persecution came)
etymology: English country, from Latin contrata, the land lying opposite, with men. The Greek genos in Paul's list means race or kindred; sumphuletes in Thessalonians means a fellow tribesman.
biblical_def: Both uses of the word in the Authorized Version stand in a list of sufferings. Paul's catalogue of perils: “In journeyings often, in perils of waters, in perils of robbers, in perils by mine own countrymen, in perils by the heathen, in perils in the city, in perils in the wilderness, in perils in the sea, in perils among false brethren” (2Co 11:26). Eight perils, and his own nation is named second — before the heathen, before the sea, before false brethren. And of the Thessalonians: “For ye, brethren, became followers of the churches of God which in Judaea are in Christ Jesus: for ye also have suffered like things of your own countrymen, even as they have of the Jews” (1Th 2:14). A Gentile church suffering from Gentile neighbours is told that it is walking the same road as the Jewish churches of Judaea suffering from their own. The pattern is constant: the sharpest opposition comes from those nearest. The Lord Jesus said it of Himself — “A prophet is not without honour, but in his own country, and among his own kin, and in his own house” (Mar 6:4) — and Paul, who was hunted by his own nation, could still write, “I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh” (Rom 9:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a countryman as one born in the same country with another; also an inhabitant of the rural parts, a husbandman.
webster_full: COUNTRYMAN, n. An inhabitant or native of a region.
2. One born in the same country with another; as, we met a countryman in a foreign land.
3. A rustic; a husbandman; a farmer.
In perils by mine own countrymen. 2 Cor. xi.
scriptures: In journeyings often, in perils of waters, in perils of robbers, in perils by mine own countrymen, in perils by the heathen, in perils in the city, in perils in the wilderness, in perils in the sea, in perils among false brethren;
For ye, brethren, became followers of the churches of God which in Judaea are in Christ Jesus: for ye also have suffered like things of your own countrymen, even as they have of the Jews:
Mar 6:4
But Jesus said unto them, A prophet is not without honour, but in his own country, and among his own kin, and in his own house.
Rom 9:3
For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh:
corruption_summary: Love of one's own nation is either abolished as a prejudice or made an idol, while Paul both suffered from his countrymen and would have been accursed for them.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 9:3 is one of the most extraordinary sentences a converted man ever wrote. Paul's countrymen had stoned him, lain in wait for him, and pursued him from city to city, and he says he could wish himself accursed from Christ for their sake. Two modern positions are equally unable to produce that sentence. The first treats natural affection for one's own people as a prejudice to be repented of, so that love of country becomes suspect in itself; Scripture will not have it, for God set the bounds of the nations, the fifth commandment reaches out to fathers and fatherland, and Christ wept over one particular city. The second position makes the nation the highest good, so that the church becomes a chaplaincy to it and the gospel is measured by what it does for the country. Paul's grief is deep precisely because he does not confuse the two: his kinsmen according to the flesh are dear to him, and their need is not political but Christ.

The catalogue in 2 Corinthians should also be allowed to correct a sentimentality about the church. Paul lists perils among false brethren in the same breath as robbers and shipwreck, and Thessalonica's persecution came from neighbours. The danger to a believer has never been chiefly from strangers; it is from those close enough to have a claim on him. That is why the Lord's word about a prophet in his own country is set in the middle of a passage about His own townsmen, who knew His mother and His brethren and were offended at Him. A Christian who finds his sharpest opposition at home, at work, or among his own people has not fallen out of the ordinary way; he has entered it, and he is in company that includes his Master.
roots_summary: Greek genos (G1085), race, kindred, nation, at 2 Corinthians 11:26; sumphuletes (G4853), a fellow tribesman, at 1 Thessalonians 2:14; sungenes (G4773), kinsman, at Romans 9:3.
roots_lines: Greek genos (G1085) — race, stock, nation; perils by mine own countrymen; 2 Corinthians 11:26.
Greek sumphuletes (G4853) — a fellow tribesman; ye suffered like things of your own countrymen; 1 Thessalonians 2:14.
Greek sungenes (G4773) — kinsman, of the same family or race; my kinsmen according to the flesh; Romans 9:3.
Greek patris (G3968) — fatherland, one's own country or town; a prophet is not without honour but in his own country; Mark 6:4.
Greek kindunos (G2794) — peril, danger; the word repeated eight times in one verse; 2 Corinthians 11:26.
usage: “In perils by mine own countrymen” — named before the heathen and the sea.
“Ye also have suffered like things of your own countrymen” — the pattern is nearness.
“I could wish that myself were accursed… for my kinsmen according to the flesh” — written by the man they hunted.

pos: n. pl. (officers who bore and tasted the king's wine; a post of trust close to the throne)
etymology: English cup with bearer. The Hebrew mashqeh is literally one who gives drink — the same word rendered butler in the account of Pharaoh's prison.
biblical_def: The plural occurs twice, both in the account of the queen of Sheba's visit, and both times among the things that took her breath away: “And the meat of his table, and the sitting of his servants, and the attendance of his ministers, and their apparel, and his cupbearers, and his ascent by which he went up unto the house of the LORD; there was no more spirit in her” (1Ki 10:5); the Chronicler repeats it almost word for word (2Ch 9:4). The office was not decorative. A cupbearer tasted what the king drank and stood nearer the throne than most princes, which is why Nehemiah's single line of self-identification is so loaded: “For I was the king's cupbearer” (Neh 1:11) — the last sentence of a prayer asking for mercy in the sight of this man. Chapter two shows him at work: “I took up the wine, and gave it unto the king. Now I had not been beforetime sad in his presence” (Neh 2:1), and that sadness, dangerous in a servant, opened the door to the rebuilding of Jerusalem. Egypt had the same office: the butler of Pharaoh who forgot Joseph two full years (Gen 40:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a cup-bearer as an attendant of a prince or at a feast, who conveys the cup or wine to the guests; an officer of the king's household.
webster_full: CUP-BEARER, n. An attendant of a prince or at a feast, who conveys wine or other liquors to the guests.
2. An officer of the king's household.
His cupbearers, and his ascent by which he went up unto the house of the Lord. 1 Kings x.
CUP, n. A small vessel of capacity, used commonly to drink out of.
scriptures: And the meat of his table, and the sitting of his servants, and the attendance of his ministers, and their apparel, and his cupbearers, and his ascent by which he went up unto the house of the LORD; there was no more spirit in her.
Neh 1:11

O Lord, I beseech thee, let now thine ear be attentive to the prayer of thy servant, and to the prayer of thy servants, who desire to fear thy name: and prosper, I pray thee, thy servant this day, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man. For I was the king's cupbearer.
Neh 2:1

And it came to pass in the month Nisan, in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes the king, that wine was before him: and I took up the wine, and gave it unto the king. Now I had not been beforetime sad in his presence.
Gen 40:1
And it came to pass after these things, that the butler of the king of Egypt and his baker had offended their lord the king of Egypt.
corruption_summary: Nehemiah is preached as a leadership manual, when the book turns on a servant in a pagan court whose prayer is four months old before he opens his mouth.
corruption_paragraphs: Nehemiah has been mined for management principles — vision, planning, delegation, dealing with opposition — and the principles are genuinely there, because Scripture is not less practical than the manuals. What the treatment tends to lose is the man's position. Nehemiah was a captive people's son holding a trusted post in the court of the empire that held them, and his one qualification for the work was proximity: he handed the king his wine. He heard the report about Jerusalem in Chislev and did not speak to Artaxerxes until Nisan, four months later, and the intervening time was spent fasting, weeping and praying. When he finally does speak, his prayer is a breath long — so I prayed to the God of heaven — because the long praying was already done. Leadership drawn from this book without the four months has taken the shape and left out the substance.

The office itself preaches. A cupbearer's duty was to taste first: whatever was in the cup reached him before it reached the king. That is a picture the New Testament fills, for the cup of God's wrath was drunk by the Son before it could touch His people, and He prayed in the garden that if it were possible the cup might pass from Him. The queen of Sheba lost her spirit at Solomon's cupbearers among his other glories, and the Lord Jesus said that a greater than Solomon is here. The last thing to notice is Nehemiah's countenance. He had never been sad before the king, and he was sore afraid when the king asked him why; a servant's face in that court was a matter of life. God used a moment of visible grief, which the man had not planned and could not hide, to open a gate for a ruined city.
roots_summary: Hebrew mashqeh (H4945), one who gives drink — cupbearer or butler; from shaqah, to give to drink; the same office in Solomon's court, Pharaoh's prison, and Artaxerxes' palace.
roots_lines: Hebrew mashqeh (H4945) — a cupbearer, a butler; Solomon's cupbearers and Nehemiah's office; 1 Kings 10:5, Nehemiah 1:11.
Hebrew shaqah (H8248) — to give drink, to water; the root of the office.
Hebrew kos (H3563) — a cup; the cup of trembling, and the cup of salvation; Isaiah 51:17, Psalm 116:13.
Hebrew ruach (H7307) — spirit, breath; there was no more spirit in the queen of Sheba; 1 Kings 10:5.
Greek poterion (G4221) — a cup; let this cup pass from me; Matthew 26:39.
usage: “His cupbearers, and his ascent… there was no more spirit in her” — the office among Solomon's glories.
“For I was the king's cupbearer” — the last line of a four-month prayer.
“I had not been beforetime sad in his presence” — a face that could have cost him his life.

pos: n. pl. (players on the harp; in Revelation, the sound of heaven and the silence of a fallen city)
etymology: From harp, Old English hearpe. The Greek kitharodos is one who sings to the kithara — a player and singer at once, which is how the Authorized Version's harpers are described.
biblical_def: The word occurs twice in Revelation, once in heaven and once over a ruin. In heaven: “And I heard a voice from heaven, as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of a great thunder: and I heard the voice of harpers harping with their harps” (Rev 14:2). Three comparisons are heaped up — waters, thunder, harps — volume and sweetness together, and the singers are the hundred and forty and four thousand who sing a new song that no man could learn but they. Earlier John sees those who had gotten the victory over the beast standing on a sea of glass “having the harps of God” (Rev 15:2). Then the silence: “And the voice of harpers, and musicians, and of pipers, and trumpeters, shall be heard no more at all in thee; and no craftsman, of whatsoever craft he be, shall be found any more in thee; and the sound of a millstone shall be heard no more at all in thee” (Rev 18:22). Music, craft and bread all stop together in Babylon. Between the two stands the exile's refusal: “We hanged our harps upon the willows in the midst thereof” (Psa 137:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a harper as a player on the harp; and the harp as one of the most ancient stringed instruments, used by the Hebrews in worship and by the ancient bards.
webster_full: HARP, n. An instrument of music of the stringed kind, of a triangular figure, held upright and struck with the fingers.
2. A constellation.
HARPER, n. A player on the harp.
I heard the voice of harpers harping with their harps. Rev. xiv.
scriptures: Rev 14:2
And I heard a voice from heaven, as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of a great thunder: and I heard the voice of harpers harping with their harps:
Rev 15:2

And I saw as it were a sea of glass mingled with fire: and them that had gotten the victory over the beast, and over his image, and over his mark, and over the number of his name, stand on the sea of glass, having the harps of God.

And the voice of harpers, and musicians, and of pipers, and trumpeters, shall be heard no more at all in thee; and no craftsman, of whatsoever craft he be, shall be found any more in thee; and the sound of a millstone shall be heard no more at all in thee;
We hanged our harps upon the willows in the midst thereof.
corruption_summary: Revelation 14 is used to settle arguments about instruments in worship, though the vision describes heaven and the New Testament nowhere commands an instrument for the church's assembly.
corruption_paragraphs: The harpers of Revelation are pressed into service on both sides of a long-standing question and prove less than either party wants. Those who wish instruments in corporate worship cite the harps of heaven; those who exclude them answer that a vision of the heavenly city is not a directory for the Lord's Day assembly, and that the New Testament, which regulates worship in detail, is silent about instruments. The regulative principle is the right frame for the discussion: what God has commanded is required, and what He has not commanded is not to be imposed. Honest men in the Reformed churches have differed on whether the silence forbids or merely leaves free, and the dictionary follows the confessional standard in holding that worship is bounded by God's appointment rather than by taste. What is not in dispute is that the singing is commanded, that it is congregational, and that the psalms are given for it.

The more searching use of the word is Revelation 18, and it is easy to miss because it sounds like an inventory. Harpers, musicians, pipers, trumpeters — no more at all. Craftsmen of every craft — not found any more. The sound of a millstone — heard no more. The candle, the bridegroom, the bride: all gone. What God takes from Babylon is not her sins in the abstract but her music, her workmanship, her bread and her weddings, the ordinary sweetness of a city; and He takes them because she had made merchandise of the souls of men. That is a warning to any culture that assumes its art will outlast its wickedness. Psalm 137 shows the other side, where the exiles hang up their harps rather than sing the LORD's song for the entertainment of their captors — and the church has been in that position more than once.
roots_summary: Greek kitharodos (G2790), one who plays and sings to the harp; kithara (G2788), the harp; Hebrew kinnowr (H3658), the harp of David and of the exiles.
roots_lines: Greek kitharodos (G2790) — a harper, one who sings to the harp; Revelation 14:2, Revelation 18:22.
Greek kithara (G2788) — the harp; the harps of God held by those who overcame the beast; Revelation 15:2.
Hebrew kinnowr (H3658) — a harp or lyre; David's instrument before Saul, and the harps hung on the willows; 1 Samuel 16:23, Psalm 137:2.
Hebrew shiyr chadash — a new song; sung before the throne and learned by none but the redeemed; Revelation 14:3, Psalm 96:1.
Greek phone (G5456) — a voice, a sound; used three times in one verse of waters, thunder and harps; Revelation 14:2.
usage: “The voice of harpers harping with their harps” — waters, thunder and sweetness together.
“Shall be heard no more at all in thee” — music, craft and bread taken from a city at once.
“We hanged our harps upon the willows” — a song refused to captors.

pos: n. (one who has killed a man; in the law, the man who killed at unawares and might flee to a city of refuge)
etymology: English man with slayer. The Hebrew ratsach is the verb of the sixth commandment; the law distinguishes by intent between the murderer, who dies, and the manslayer, who flees.
biblical_def: The law of Israel drew a line the modern conscience often blurs. Six of the Levites' cities were set apart “for the manslayer, that he may flee thither” (Num 35:6), and the case is defined: “that the slayer may flee thither, which killeth any person at unawares” (Num 35:11). The refuge is not an evasion of justice but the guarantee of it: “And they shall be unto you cities for refuge from the avenger; that the manslayer die not, until he stand before the congregation in judgment” (Num 35:12). He must be tried. If the killing was with hatred, he dies; if at unawares, he lives, but not freely — “he shall abide in it unto the death of the high priest, which was anointed with the holy oil” (Num 35:25). Blood has been shed and the land is not clean until a death occurs; the death that releases him is the high priest's. The type is not accidental. The man who has taken a life and cannot go home is set at liberty by the death of an anointed priest — and the New Testament names the High Priest whose death opens every gate.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a manslayer as one that has slain a human being; and manslaughter, in law, as the unlawful killing of a man without malice, express or implied — distinguished from murder.
webster_full: MANSLAYER, n. One that has slain a human being.
MANSLAUGHTER, n. In law, the unlawful killing of a man without malice, express or implied.
This may be voluntary, upon a sudden heat, or involuntary, in the commission of an unlawful act.
Cities for refuge… for the manslayer. Num. xxxv.
scriptures: Then ye shall appoint you cities to be cities of refuge for you; that the slayer may flee thither, which killeth any person at unawares.
And they shall be unto you cities for refuge from the avenger; that the manslayer die not, until he stand before the congregation in judgment.

And the congregation shall deliver the slayer out of the hand of the revenger of blood, and the congregation shall restore him to the city of his refuge, whither he was fled: and he shall abide in it unto the death of the high priest, which was anointed with the holy oil.
Rev 15:2

And I saw as it were a sea of glass mingled with fire: and them that had gotten the victory over the beast, and over his image, and over his mark, and over the number of his name, stand on the sea of glass, having the harps of God.
corruption_summary: Intent has been made either everything or nothing in modern thinking about killing, while the law of refuge weighs intent carefully and still requires a death before the land is clean.
corruption_paragraphs: The cities of refuge answer two errors at once. The first collapses all killing into one category, so that any taking of life is murder and no distinction of intent is allowed; the law refuses this, providing a road, a city and a trial for the man who killed at unawares, and Deuteronomy adds the case of the axe head flying from the helve. The second error is the reverse, and it is the more common now: intent is made the whole matter, so that a man who did not mean it is held to owe nothing at all. The law refuses that too. The manslayer is not acquitted and sent home; he leaves his house, his fields and his standing, and lives in a city not his own until the high priest dies. Guilt and liability are not identical, and Scripture keeps both. A life has been ended, and the accounting does not vanish because the heart was innocent of malice.

The release is what makes the statute gospel rather than mere jurisprudence. The manslayer's term is not fixed by years or by good behaviour; it ends at the death of the high priest, and at no other event. He waits for a death he did not cause and cannot hasten, and that death sets him free to return to the land of his possession. Hebrews takes up the whole apparatus — a High Priest anointed not with oil but by the Spirit, who entered once into the holy place having obtained eternal redemption — and the epistle even uses the figure of fleeing for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us. The city gate stood open and the roads were kept clear by law so that no man's flight should fail for want of a way. That is how the gospel is to be preached: plainly enough that a man running for his life can find it.
roots_summary: Hebrew ratsach (H7523), to slay or murder — the verb of the sixth commandment, used both of the murderer and of the manslayer; with miqlat (H4733), a refuge, and goel haddam, the avenger of blood.
roots_lines: Hebrew ratsach (H7523) — to slay; thou shalt not kill, and the slayer that killeth at unawares; Exodus 20:13, Numbers 35:11.
Hebrew miqlat (H4733) — a refuge, an asylum; the six cities appointed among the Levites; Numbers 35:6.
Hebrew goel (H1350) — a redeemer, a kinsman; here the avenger of blood, the same word as kinsman-redeemer; Numbers 35:12.
Hebrew bishgagah — at unawares, by error; the phrase that divides manslaughter from murder; Numbers 35:11.
Greek archiereus (G749) — high priest; whose death released the manslayer, and whose antitype released the guilty; Hebrews 9:11.
usage: “That the manslayer die not, until he stand before the congregation in judgment” — refuge as the guarantee of trial.
“Which killeth any person at unawares” — intent weighed, and liability kept.
“Unto the death of the high priest” — a release no prisoner could hasten.

pos: n. pl. (persons held as security for the performance of terms; taken from Judah after a battle her king had provoked)
etymology: Old French hostage, from Latin obses, one given as a pledge. The Hebrew taarubah comes from arab, to pledge or give surety — the same root behind the word for a man who stands as security for another.
biblical_def: The word occurs once, at the end of a war Amaziah of Judah had picked: “And he took all the gold and the silver, and all the vessels that were found in the house of God with Obededom, and the treasures of the king's house, the hostages also, and returned to Samaria” (2Ch 25:24). Joash of Israel had warned him in a parable of a thistle and a cedar and told him plainly to stay at home; Amaziah would not hear, was beaten at Bethshemesh, and Jerusalem's wall was broken down four hundred cubits. The vessels of the house of God went north, and so did living pledges — men and boys held to guarantee that Judah would keep terms. The chapter says why the king would not listen: it came of God, that he might deliver them into the hand of their enemies, because they sought after the gods of Edom. A pledge in Scripture is a solemn thing; the word's root is the same as that behind standing surety, and Judah, who had refused to be warned, ended by leaving her sons in another king's hand as the price of a war she chose.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a hostage as a person delivered to an enemy or hostile power, as a pledge to secure the performance of the conditions of a treaty.
webster_full: HOSTAGE, n. A person delivered to an enemy or hostile power, as a pledge to secure the performance of the conditions of a treaty or stipulations of any kind.
2. Hostages were formerly given by princes as a security for the payment of tribute.
The treasures of the king's house, the hostages also. 2 Chron. xxv.
HOSTAGESHIP, n. The state of being a hostage.
scriptures: And he took all the gold and the silver, and all the vessels that were found in the house of God with Obededom, and the treasures of the king's house, the hostages also, and returned to Samaria.
Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.
Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established.
My lovers and my friends stand aloof from my sore; and my kinsmen stand afar off.
corruption_summary: The chapter is read as a story about a proud king, and its plainest lesson is skipped — that other people paid for what Amaziah refused to hear.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a leader's refusal of counsel is paid for by people who never sat in the room. Amaziah was warned by an enemy king, in a parable, and the warning was sound; he would not hear it, and the consequences fell on a broken wall, an emptied temple, and families whose sons went north as pledges. Scripture's two proverbs on counsel say the same thing from the other side — where no counsel is, the people fall, and in the multitude of counsellors there is safety — and both put the cost on the people rather than on the counsellor. That is the burden of office. A man who will not be advised is not merely risking himself.

There is a second thing in the account that repays attention. The Chronicler says the deafness came of God, that He might deliver them into the hand of their enemies, because Amaziah had brought home the gods of Edom and bowed himself before them. Judicial hardening is a real doctrine and it appears in exactly this shape throughout Scripture — Pharaoh's heart, Sihon's spirit, Rehoboam's ear. It never removes the man's responsibility; Amaziah is blamed and punished, and the text does not present him as a puppet. It does mean that a settled refusal to hear correction may itself be a judgment already fallen, which is a sobering thought for anyone who finds warnings easy to dismiss. The mercy in the passage is small and real: the hostages are recorded. God noticed who was carried away for another man's pride.
roots_summary: Hebrew taarubah (H8594), a pledge or hostage, from arab (H6148), to give surety, to pledge oneself for another.
roots_lines: Hebrew taarubah (H8594) — a pledge, a hostage; the hostages also, and returned to Samaria; 2 Chronicles 25:24.
Hebrew arab (H6148) — to pledge, to become surety; be surety for thy servant for good; Psalm 119:122.
Hebrew erabown (H6162) — a pledge, an earnest; Judah's pledge left with Tamar; Genesis 38:17.
Hebrew etsah (H6098) — counsel; the thing Amaziah refused; Proverbs 11:14.
Greek arrhabon (G728) — an earnest, a down payment; the Spirit given as the earnest of our inheritance; Ephesians 1:14.
usage: “The treasures of the king's house, the hostages also” — the price of a war a king chose.
“Where no counsel is, the people fall” — the cost falls on the people.
The hostages are recorded — God noticed who was carried away for another man's pride.

pos: n. (relations by blood; those nearest by nature, whose failure Scripture records without softening)
etymology: English kin, family, with folk, people. The Hebrew qarowb means simply the near ones; the Greek sungenes is those of the same stock.
biblical_def: Job names their failure among his losses: “My kinsfolk have failed, and my familiar friends have forgotten me” (Job 19:14), and the verse before it says who arranged it — “He hath put my brethren far from me, and mine acquaintance are verily estranged from me” (Job 19:13). David knows the same distance: “My lovers and my friends stand aloof from my sore; and my kinsmen stand afar off” (Psa 38:11). Both men are describing what suffering does to a circle of relations, and both attribute it, finally, to God's hand rather than merely to human coldness. Luke uses the word in one of the quietest and most human verses in the Gospels: Joseph and Mary, returning from the feast, “supposing him to have been in the company, went a day's journey; and they sought him among their kinsfolk and acquaintance” (Luk 2:44). They looked for the Son of God among the relatives, which is where a boy would be. And the Lord Himself said that a prophet is without honour “among his own kin, and in his own house” (Mar 6:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines kinsfolk as relations; kindred; persons of the same family; and kin as relation, properly by consanguinity or blood.
webster_full: KIN, n. Relation, properly by consanguinity or blood; kindred.
2. Relations; kindred; persons of the same race or family.
KINSFOLK, n. Relations; kindred; persons of the same family.
My kinsfolk have failed, and my familiar friends have forgotten me. Job xix.
scriptures: My kinsfolk have failed, and my familiar friends have forgotten me.
He hath put my brethren far from me, and mine acquaintance are verily estranged from me.
My lovers and my friends stand aloof from my sore; and my kinsmen stand afar off.
Luk 2:44
But they, supposing him to have been in the company, went a day's journey; and they sought him among their kinsfolk and acquaintance.
corruption_summary: Two errors stand opposite each other — family made an absolute good, and family treated as optional — while Scripture honours the tie, records its failures, and puts Christ above it.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture holds the natural family in the highest honour. The fifth commandment stands in the first table's shadow with a promise attached; a man who does not provide for his own house has denied the faith; children are a heritage of the LORD. And the same Scripture is entirely unsentimental about what families are actually like. Job's kinsfolk failed him; David's kinsmen stood afar off from his sore; Joseph's brethren sold him; the Lord's own brethren did not believe on Him until after the resurrection. The corruption to name is a religious idealisation of family life in which the household is spoken of as if it were a means of grace, and any admission of its failures is felt as disloyalty. Job 19 is in the canon so that a believer whose relations have failed him need not conclude that his experience is outside Scripture.

The opposite corruption is now the louder one, and it treats blood ties as arrangements a man may set down when they no longer suit him — parents kept at a chosen distance, siblings dropped, obligations reassigned to friends selected for agreement. Christ does relativise the family, and He does it more sharply than any modern writer: he that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and He asked, who is my mother? But the relativising is toward Him and toward the household of faith, not toward a man's own preference; and the same Lord provided for His mother from the cross and rebuked the Pharisees for using a religious vow to avoid supporting their parents. Luke 2:44 keeps the whole matter human. Two tired parents walked a day's journey assuming their boy was among the relations, and had to go back to Jerusalem to find Him in the temple — the first recorded instance of the truth that Christ is not found merely by being among one's own people.
roots_summary: Hebrew qarowb (H7138), near ones, kinsfolk; meyudda (H3045), familiar friends, the known ones; Greek sungenes (G4773), kindred.
roots_lines: Hebrew qarowb (H7138) — near, at hand, a near kinsman; my kinsfolk have failed; Job 19:14.
Hebrew meyudda — the known ones, familiar friends; joined to kinsfolk in Job's complaint; Job 19:14.
Hebrew goel (H1350) — the kinsman-redeemer, the near relation with a right to redeem; Ruth 3:9, Leviticus 25:25.
Greek sungenes (G4773) — of the same stock, kindred; they sought him among their kinsfolk and acquaintance; Luke 2:44.
Greek patris (G3968) — one's own country; a prophet is without honour among his own kin; Mark 6:4.
usage: “My kinsfolk have failed” — and the verse before names whose hand did it.
“My kinsmen stand afar off” — the distance suffering makes.
“They sought him among their kinsfolk and acquaintance” — and He was not there.
